newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ANZ to launch emerging market debt fund.
newsitem.headline: ANZ to launch emerging market debt fund.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd's Funds Management arm said on Thursday it aimed initially to attract A$50 million to A$100 million into an emerging markets debt fund it would launch in August.
The fund will have a minimum investment of A$500,000 and target high net worth individuals and superannuation funds, ANZ Funds Management said.

The new fund would mirror the investment policies of ANZ's Emerging Market Liquid Investment Portfolio (EMLIP), an emerging market debt fund set up by ANZ Investment Bank in London in 1992 for rich individuals and funds.

EMLIP, a U.S. dollar fund, had returned an annual average compound rate of return of 25.22 percent since 1992 and had never made an annual return of less than 10 percent over any one of those years, ANZ said.
This compared with compound annual returns from the JP Morgan Brady Bond index of 19.79 percent over the same period.
EMLIP currently had about US$700 million in funds under management.

ANZ Funds Management chief investment officer Glenn Woolley said the fund was aimed mainly at corporates and institutional investors, although rich individuals could access the fund through ANZ Investment Bank.
He said investors were looking for higher returns as yields fell in more established bond markets and as equity markets reached their peaks.
"People are increasingly looking to make profits in emerging markets and to put it into other asset classes," Woolley said.
About 60 percent of the funds in EMLIP come from rich individuals, particularly in the Middle East where ANZ has a strong presence through its ANZ Grindlays arm.
About 40 percent comes from institutional investors.
EMLIP currently invests in 25 countries and in over 50 different sovereign instruments, ranging from Panama through Bulgaria to Russia.
EMLIP had about 20 percent of its funds invested in Russian debt and 13 percent in Mexican debt.
ANZ Emerging Markets Funds Management director John Cartwright said the new fund aimed to emulate EMLIP in investing across emerging markets.
He said the fund would try to invest in bonds that had potential for capital growth bought on by lowering inflation rates and economic reform in certain countries as well as high yield.
Those non-performing bonds bought were often bought at major discounts and stood to gain when a country was reformed and started repaying debt again, he said.
Cartwright said the world's pension funds were just starting to hunt around outside the major debt markets for higher yields as low inflation bought down yields.
Pension funds currently had about two to three percent of their funds in emerging markets and many were now looking to push that up to five to ten percent, he said.
"There's still a lot of money coming into these markets searching for yield," Cartwright told the briefing.
The fund charges a management fee of 1.25 percent of net asset value and has an incentive fee of 25 percent of the return when it exceeds 15 percent. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
